text.en: Find the notes of line 1: each one waits until you're on it.
It's a halyard shanty, for hoisting heavy yards. The crew rested on the rope while the shantyman sang his line, then took a big pull together as they roared the refrain.

source.en: Mainly Norfolk, "Blow the Man Down" (A.L. Lloyd songs; Topic Records sleeve notes)

text.en: Hear line 1, then sing it back.
Hear line 2, then sing it back.
Now lines 1 and 2 joined: hear them, then sing them back.
Hear line 3, then sing it back.
Hear line 4, then sing it back.
Line 5 is the tune of line 1 again, with new words. Sing it with the guide.
Line 6 is line 2 again. Sing it with the guide.
Now lines 3 to 6 joined, with the guide.
Line 7 is the tune of line 3 again, with new words. Sing it with the guide.
Line 8 is line 4 again. Sing it with the guide.
Line 9 is the tune of line 1 again, with new words. Sing it with the guide.
Line 10 is line 2 again. Sing it with the guide.
Now lines 7 to 10 joined, with the guide.
Hear line 11, then sing it back.
Hear line 12, then sing it back.
Now lines 11 and 12 joined, with the guide.
The call start to end, with the guide.
Verse 1 start to end, with the guide.
Verse 2 start to end, with the guide.
The whole song, with the guide.
Sing your part with the other parts, and the guide with you. Hold your line while the others move.
The guide drops out: your part with the others only. Give me my note plays your first note quietly.
Once more on your own, from the top.
Record the tune of Blow the Man Down in Sing, with the other parts playing.
The earliest known trace of it is from July 1867, in a Syracuse newspaper, the Daily Courier.
